question: Tell me about a situation where a team member was not pulling their weight. What did you do?

raiseTranscript.text: On my first project after onboarding, one teammate kept missing daily standup updates and left their part of the shared doc empty. I waited two days then asked them in a private chat if they were blocked on anything.
They said they were unclear on the requirements. I walked them through the spec and offered to pair on the first section. They finished their piece by the end of the week and thanked me in the retro.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where a team member was not pulling their weight. What did you do?
Role: new grad on 4-person feature team
Situation: peer missed updates and left doc section blank
Action: private check-in, offered to clarify requirements and pair
Outcome: work completed on time; peer thanked them in retro
Quote: "I waited two days then asked them in a private chat if they were blocked"
Follow-up: Did you tell the manager? No, I wanted to try solving it directly first
junior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Junior. The candidate described a local teamwork issue with a peer who missed updates on a shared doc. They chose a private 1:1 check-in, clarified requirements, and offered to pair, resulting in on-time delivery and a positive retro mention. This shows appropriate junior-level ownership and coachability without escalating unnecessarily. The story is small in scope but demonstrates learning to address friction directly rather than ignoring it or going around the person. Biggest strength is the calm, low-drama approach that stayed within their individual sphere of control.

lowerTranscript.text: Yeah there was this one guy who never did his part on the group assignment. I just did it myself so the project wouldn't slip.
Did you talk to him about it?
Not really, I didn't want to cause drama. I just finished the section and moved on.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where a team member was not pulling their weight. What did you do?

Situation: teammate skipped their section
Action: completed the work themselves without conversation
Outcome: project delivered but no resolution with teammate
Quote: "I just did it myself so the project wouldn't slip"
Follow-up: Any follow-up after? No, semester ended
junior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Junior. The candidate responded to a non-contributing teammate by silently completing the missing work themselves. They avoided any direct conversation to prevent drama and did not attempt to understand the root cause or involve others. This shows limited ownership of team dynamics and misses the opportunity to practice basic collaboration skills expected even at entry level. The outcome left the underlying issue unaddressed. Biggest gap is the absence of any attempt at direct, low-stakes communication.

raiseTranscript.text: A backend engineer on another team kept delivering late on shared API work, blocking two of my services. I pulled the last three sprints of data showing the pattern and asked for a 1:1.
I shared the impact numbers and asked what support they needed. We agreed on smaller PRs and a weekly sync. Their on-time rate went from 40% to 85% over the next quarter.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where a team member was not pulling their weight. What did you do?
Role: senior on platform team
Situation: cross-team dependency consistently late
Action: gathered metrics, held 1:1, proposed smaller chunks and weekly sync
Outcome: on-time delivery rose to 85%
Quote: "I pulled the last three sprints of data showing the pattern"
Follow-up: Did their manager get involved? Only after we had a working agreement in place
senior.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Senior. The candidate addressed repeated late deliveries from a cross-team engineer by collecting concrete metrics and initiating a data-driven 1:1 conversation. They proposed practical adjustments such as smaller PRs and a weekly sync, lifting on-time performance from 40% to 85%. This demonstrates influence without authority and measurable cross-team impact. The approach stayed constructive and focused on shared outcomes rather than blame. Biggest strength is the use of data to create leverage and the willingness to invest in an ongoing coordination mechanism.

lowerTranscript.text: There was a contractor on another team who was slow. I escalated to their manager and to my director after the second late handoff.
What did you try before escalating?
I sent a couple of Slack messages asking for status. When nothing changed I went to the managers.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where a team member was not pulling their weight. What did you do?
Role: senior engineer
Situation: contractor missing deadlines on shared work
Action: sent status pings then escalated to two managers
Outcome: issue handed off; no direct resolution attempted
Quote: "I sent a couple of Slack messages asking for status"
Follow-up: Did you offer any help or alternatives? No, I assumed it was their manager's job
senior.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Senior. The candidate moved quickly from a few Slack status requests to escalation involving two managers without attempting a direct conversation or exploring root causes. They treated the problem as someone else's responsibility rather than using their senior scope to influence outcomes across teams. The story lacks evidence of building relationships or creating sustainable fixes. Biggest gap is the absence of influence-without-authority skills expected at this level.

raiseTranscript.text: One of my reports was consistently missing sprint commitments while the rest of the team was carrying extra load. I pulled them into a private meeting with specific examples from the last two sprints.

We set a 30-day performance plan with clear weekly check-ins and paired them with a senior peer for the first two weeks. After the period their velocity normalized and the team stopped having to re-plan around them.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where a team member was not pulling their weight. What did you do?
Role: engineering manager of 8
Situation: direct report missing commitments, creating team drag
Action: private meeting with examples, created 30-day plan with peer support
Outcome: velocity normalized; team no longer replanning around them
Quote: "We set a 30-day performance plan with clear weekly check-ins"
Follow-up: Did the person improve long-term? Yes, stayed solid for the next two quarters
manager.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Manager. The candidate identified a direct report whose missed commitments were forcing the rest of the team to absorb extra work. They held a documented private conversation, implemented a structured 30-day plan with weekly check-ins and peer pairing, and restored balanced team velocity. This shows clear ownership of team outcomes and appropriate use of performance management tools. The approach balanced support with accountability. Biggest strength is turning an individual performance issue into restored team leverage without drama.

lowerTranscript.text: I had a low performer on the team. I gave them feedback in the annual review and hoped things would get better.
Did you do anything between reviews?
I mentioned it a few times in 1:1s but didn't put anything formal in place. Eventually the team just worked around them.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where a team member was not pulling their weight. What did you do?
Role: manager of 7
Situation: underperforming report
Action: mentioned issue sporadically in 1:1s and annual review
Outcome: team worked around the person; no formal plan
Quote: "I gave them feedback in the annual review and hoped things would get better"
Follow-up: Any measurable change? No
manager.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Manager. The candidate addressed underperformance only through occasional 1:1 mentions and an annual review, allowing the rest of the team to absorb the shortfall indefinitely. They did not implement a performance plan, set clear expectations with timelines, or protect team capacity. This reflects weak ownership of team outcomes and underuse of standard management levers. Biggest gap is the failure to create accountability or leverage for the broader team.

raiseTranscript.text: Two product teams were consistently under-delivering because one shared platform team was overloaded and deprioritizing their requests. I commissioned a capacity review across the three teams and shifted two headcount to the platform group while changing intake rules.
Platform throughput increased 35% in the following quarter and the two product teams hit their roadmap targets for the first time in a year. We also reduced cross-team escalations by half.

raiseNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where a team member was not pulling their weight. What did you do?
Role: VP Engineering, org of 120
Situation: platform team bottleneck affecting multiple product teams
Action: capacity review, reallocated two headcount, changed intake process
Outcome: 35% throughput lift; product teams hit roadmap; 50% fewer escalations
Quote: "I commissioned a capacity review across the three teams"
Follow-up: How did the platform team feel about the change? They had asked for headcount for six months; this resolved it
exec.raiseFeedback: Raises the bar for Exec. The candidate recognized that repeated under-delivery stemmed from an overloaded platform team rather than individual failings. They ran an org-level capacity review, reallocated two headcount, and updated intake rules, producing a 35% throughput increase and allowing product teams to meet roadmap targets. This demonstrates strategic judgment on structural causes and long-term leverage over heroics. The fix addressed root capacity and process rather than symptoms. Biggest strength is translating a recurring collaboration failure into an org design change with measurable business impact.

lowerTranscript.text: We had a platform team that kept dropping the ball for product teams. I told the platform manager to fix it and followed up in staff meetings.
Not really. The product teams learned to plan extra buffer time. I moved on to other priorities.

lowerNotes: Q: Tell me about a situation where a team member was not pulling their weight. What did you do?

Quote: "I told the platform manager to fix it and followed up in staff meetings"

exec.lowerFeedback: Lowers the bar for Exec. The candidate delegated a systemic collaboration failure to a single manager and relied on staff-meeting reminders without providing resources or changing org structure. Product teams adapted by adding buffers rather than the root issue being resolved. This shows limited strategic ownership and an absence of leverage thinking at the org level. Biggest gap is treating a structural capacity problem as a local management issue.
